Date: 2025-06-27
Time: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 58 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Miguel Ortega (Redwood SE), Jin Park (Redwood Infra), Lena Morris (Horizon Head of Platform), Arjun Patel (Horizon SRE), Dmitri Kozlov (Horizon ML Infra), Sofia Ruiz (Horizon Security)
summary: Technical deep dive on prefix/prompt caching strategies: cache key design, tenant isolation and eviction policies, hit-rate tradeoffs, batching interplay, and quantization impacts for on-prem/VPC pilots. Agreed to run targeted microbenchmarks and share eviction/playbook doc. Horizon provided traffic samples for pilot gating.
transcript:
[00:00] Samira: hey everyone, thanks for carving out time, we'll dig into the eviction and coherence stuff around prefix caching. Uh Miguel and Jin are here to cover infra details.
[00:12] Lena: great, we sent over the traffic sample bundle yesterday, hope it landed in your inbox.
[00:18] Miguel: yep saw it, arjun's CSV was helpful. Quick note, I'll call the cache the KV cache but you'll hear people say KV cash or prefix cash in transcripts so ignore that.
[00:30] Arjun: haha noted. Our main worry is hot-tenants dominating mem footprint, we need a safe eviction policy that won't regress tail latency.
[00:43] Jin: right, so today we'll run through keying strategies, TTLs, LRU vs LFU, and also the consistent hashing shard boundaries we use in dedicated pools.
[00:55] Dmitri: can you define 'prefix' for the purposes of this talk? we have short prompts and some long system-level context, do both get cached?
[01:05] Miguel: good question. Redwood distinguishes prefix caching for long, high-reuse context (system prompts, user history snippets) and prompt-level caching for complete prompts. The key composition we recommend is: model_id|session_type|normalized_prefix_hash|token_length_bucket. In practice we normalize whitespace, canonicalize system tokens, and strip transient timestamps.
[01:30] Lena: we have many multi-tenant users where prefixes vary only by tenant ID or customer metadata. how do you avoid leakage or collisions?
[01:38] Miguel: tenant_id is included in the key by default for multi-tenant mode. But you can opt into shared-prefix mode where the tenant_id is omitted for cross-tenant caching if you trust similarity and data policies. For Horizon we assume isolating tenants at first.
[01:55] Sofia: from security standpoint we require per-tenant isolation and audit logs; anything that shares across tenants needs legal sign-off.
[02:03] Samira: noted. So default: tenant-scoped keys. We also support namespace-level RBAC so operations teams can see hit/miss metrics per tenant.
[02:15] Arjun: about the hash, collisions worry me at scale — what's your collision mitigation?
[02:21] Jin: we use 128-bit hashes (xxhash128) plus a short prefix fingerprint. On a collision the runtime checks the un-hashed normalized blob to confirm a true match before returning. There is a small CPU cost but avoids incorrect replays.
[02:38] Dmitri: ok that helps. now eviction: we saw earlier docs mentioning priority buckets, can you expand?
[02:45] Miguel: yes. We have three eviction classes: pinned (hot, explicit TTL override), transient (short TTLs, user session context), and shared (longer TTL for system prompts). Inside each class we can run either LRU or LFU. For Horizon we suggested LFU for shared system prompts and LRU for transient session contexts.
[03:05] Lena: how do we detect a "hot tenant"? do you have per-tenant admission controls?
[03:12] Jin: we expose metrics: per-tenant cache footprint, hit rate, miss penalty (avg extra tokens generated due to miss), and eviction churn. You can set soft limits per-tenant and an autoscaler that will eject low-value entries when a tenant crosses its budget.
[03:27] Arjun: curious about the miss penalty metric — how is that measured?
[03:31] Miguel: miss penalty is measured as the extra end-to-end latency and token count when the prefix isn't in KV cache and the model must re-run the prefix. For example with a 32k context GPT-style model, a miss for a long prefix can add 150-300ms and X tokens of compute. We instrument per-request: cached_prefix_tokens vs recompute_tokens, and attribute cost.
[03:55] Dmitri: what about batching? if a miss happens, does it break your batching and cause head-of-line delays?
[04:02] Jin: yes this is important. We do continuous batching at the runtime layer; misses can be prefetchable in some cases. Two strategies: synchronous miss (slow path) and asynchronous prefetch (we return partial/streamed while we prefetch the remainder). For high-throughput endpoints we prefer async prefetch and partial streaming to keep latency SLOs.
[04:25] Lena: can you give an example with numbers?
[04:28] Miguel: sure. With batch size of 16 on A100s, a cached prefix can shave ~30-60ms per request compared to recomputing the prefix. But a cold miss that triggers recomputation can add a 200-400ms penalty and also reduce effective batch size for a few cycles while KV warms. So hit rate matters a lot.
[04:50] Arjun: what's a realistic hit rate target for multi-tenant workloads?
[04:54] Miguel: depends on prompt shape. For session-heavy workloads we often see 65-85% hit rates; for many ad-hoc prompts it's lower, 30-50%. For Horizon's telemetry your sample looked promising for a pilot with expected 70% hit rate on system prompts.
[05:10] Dmitri: and what's the rule-of-thumb for TTLs?
[05:13] Miguel: system prompts: hours to days; session prefixes: seconds to minutes; user history: configurable and often pinned per session. But TTL interacts with eviction policy and memory limits — shorter TTL reduces footprint but hurts hit rate.
[05:27] Sofia: quantization — does using int8/4 quantized models affect the cache semantics or reproducibility of outputs?
[05:34] Miguel: quantization itself doesn't change the prefix hashing or cache keys. But it can change generation outcomes slightly which matters for QA/regression. We tag cache entries with model_variant (e.g., gptx-32k-f32 vs gptx-32k-ptq8) so we never return an entry generated under a different quantization profile.
[05:55] Lena: nice. so when we roll new quantized builds we won't accidentally serve old outputs.
[05:59] Miguel: exact. Also note that quantized models are faster and smaller, which can change the economics: if recompute cost becomes cheap, the value of cache diminishes for certain prefixes.
[06:12] Arjun: network for VPC/on-prem: we are testing Private deployment behind our VPC and our KMS is on-prem HSM. Does that change caching design?
[06:21] Jin: network limits can increase miss penalty; if your runtime can't access a centralized KV store fast, we recommend local per-node cache shards with bloom filters for global membership. For HSM/KMS keys we only use them for control plane and encryption at rest; they don't affect lookup latency but might add handshake on startup.
[06:40] Dmitri: local shards — then how do you ensure coherence across nodes? what about consistency windows?
[06:45] Miguel: we accept eventual consistency for prefix caches. The system uses a lease-based invalidation for pinned updates (e.g., policy change) and periodic background syncs. Coherence is measured by the staleness window metric. If you need strict coherence you can disable local shards and use a central high-throughput KV with cross-region replication, but that has latency tradeoffs.
[07:05] Lena: what about evicting by value vs time? e.g., if a tenant's prefixes generate low reuse but high compute, will you evict them proactively?
[07:13] Jin: yes we have a cost-aware eviction score: score = alpha * (reuse_rate) - beta * (compute_cost_per_recompute) - gamma * (tenant_priority). This lets you prefer evicting low-reuse, high-cost entries. We tune alpha/beta/gamma per workload.
[07:31] Arjun: that sounds powerful but also complex to tune. how do you recommend we start?
[07:36] Miguel: start with simple heuristics: enforce per-tenant memory quotas, set system/shared TTLs to longer values, and run LFU for shared. After 1-2 weeks of metrics, enable cost-aware eviction with conservative weights. We'll provide an initial config for Horizon.
[07:54] Dmitri: do you have instrumentation dashboards we can plug into Grafana?
[07:58] Jin: yes. We export Prometheus metrics: keystore_hit_rate, per_tenant_hit_rate, miss_penalty_ms, eviction_churn_rate, cache_footprint_bytes. We also ship a sample Grafana dashboard (link shared).
[08:12] Samira: linking the playbook here: https://rbwd.co/prefix-eviction-playbook (internal) — contains suggested configs for pilot.
[08:19] Lena: thank you. a few follow-ups: can you show how cache keys are normalized for whitespace and for user-specific tokens, and can we get a sample of raw vs normalized keys?
[08:30] Miguel: yes — we'll include a sample mapping in the doc. Also note we support redact-and-hash patterns so PII can be removed before hashing.
[08:41] Sofia: on compliance, we need audit logs for cache hits that include tenant_id and request_id and a hash — does Redwood capture that?
[08:47] Jin: we log hit events with tenant_id, truncated key hash, request_id, and timestamp. We can increase retention for enterprise accounts.
[08:56] Arjun: one more operational question — if we have a spike and the runtime starts thrashing, do you have an automatic fallback to a smaller model to preserve throughput?
[09:05] Miguel: yes the smart routing layer can fallback to a cheaper model variant or route to dedicated burst capacity, and you can configure per-route fallback policies.
[09:14] Dmitri: how do we quantify the cost-benefit of caching vs adding more GPUs?
[09:19] Miguel: we produce per-prefix cost curves: cost_saved = (recompute_token_cost - cached_token_cost) * hit_rate - overhead_costs. We can run sensitivity analysis using your telemetry to estimate GPU-hours saved. We'll run that for Horizon in the pilot.
[09:34] Lena: ok. what's the proposed pilot?
[09:37] Samira: pilot plan: 4-week pilot, 3-5 tenants, use dedicated private runtime in your VPC with local shards enabled, run with LFU for shared system prompts, LRU for session context, and conservative cost-aware eviction off initially. We'll collect metrics and decide on thresholds end of week 2.
[09:57] Arjun: sounds good. any security blockers?
[10:00] Sofia: need explicit notes on data-at-rest encryption, KMS handshake, and retention of hit logs. Please share compliance document.
[10:07] Samira: will do. Action items summarized in the doc.
[10:11] Miguel: quick technical caveat — prefix normalization can sometimes remove semantic tokens that change generation; we'll highlight examples and tests to ensure no regression.
[10:20] Dmitri: appreciated. last Q: do you support evicting based on custom business labels? e.g., feature flag entries we want always kept?
[10:28] Jin: yes you can pin entries via API with a label and TTL infinite or long; label-based priority is supported.
[10:35] Lena: that's all from us. thanks team.
[10:38] Samira: recap: Samira share doc; Miguel run microbenchmarks; Horizon provide data samples; schedule follow-up in one week.
[10:47] Arjun: bye all.
